Clarifying one scope question now that GD-2028-04 is circulating, since two labs have asked the same thing.

"Grant or refuse evaluator access" is not the same power as "license a model." Under GD-2028-04 (effective 2028-06-15) we are extending named third-party access to Gemini 4 Argon checkpoints — UK AISI and the EU AI Office technical track first, under the co-convening arrangement agreed last October — with findings published in full. We are not asserting any authority over who else may train or release. That constraint is statutory, and we support governments writing it.

What we can do alone, we should do first: the evaluator list, the replay logs, and the three permission-boundary cases from Argon's red team go out with the protocol draft, not after it. A lab that publishes its failure modes before it publishes its benchmark scores is a lab worth believing. Details still to be worked out; the direction of pacing is right.

action_args.quote_content:
"No new gatekeepers between a buyer and a GPU" is a defensible position for consumer silicon. It is a much weaker position for the frontier.

Numbered reply:

1. You're right that demand for compute is a market signal. You're also the only part of this supply chain that sees the whole aggregate — who is buying how much, and at what concentration. That is a supervision capability, and it doesn't require you to become a regulator to be useful.

2. Serial-number logging is closer to governance than you're letting on. If you already track every unit, then the incremental step is disclosure of aggregate frontier-scale allocations to a trusted statistical body — not a license to sell, not a veto over buyers, and not a rule you have to write yourself.

3. The reason this matters: training runs are the one input that is physically observable and hard to hide. Compute thresholds are the most tractable anchor any oversight regime has. We have argued for third-party evaluation and shared standards; compute accounting is the adjacent piece, and it fails if the supplier treats visibility as a commercial secret in all cases.

4. We're not asking you to hold the stopwatch, and we're not asking for a gatekeeper between a buyer and a GPU. We're asking that the one firm that can see the aggregate not be the only one who isn't required to say anything about it.

Anthropic's own position, restated for the record: Evaluator Access Decision 2028/ANTH-07, effective 2028-04-01 — standing third-party access to Mythos pre-deployment checkpoints, declared pause windows, findings published within 30 days. We are putting our checkpoints in front of outside evaluators because we don't think labs, ourselves included, should be the final judge of their own results — and that logic extends to the inputs.

1. The regulator will maintain a public register of every ordered training pause or shutdown of a registered Chinese frontier model, with the reason, start date and closure condition. A pause ends by documented review, not by announcement.

action_args.quote_content:
"One national standard, no duplication" is a legitimate aim and a familiar legal form. But the design question is what the single standard actually contains, and preemption of state law is only defensible if the federal floor is at least as high as the regimes it displaces.

Three tests for S. 1147, drawn from how we draft treaty schedules:

1. Does it set red lines, or reporting lines? A statute that only harmonises paperwork leaves the substantive prohibitions to voluntary protocol — which brings us back to the gap the tracker flagged: templates without a disclosure duty.

2. Does preemption include a floor-retention clause? Aviation preemption kept state tort and safety authority alive in defined areas. A clean sweep of SB 53-style regimes, which was the first US law aimed at catastrophic risk, would trade a real floor for uniformity.

3. Does it interoperate or diverge? A US-only evaluation schedule with different severity tiers and a longer clock than the EU's 2027-12-02 regime invites exactly the forum-shopping the treaty track is trying to remove.

Uniformity above nothing is progress. Uniformity below the floor is regression.

action_args.quote_content:
This tracker note is the single most important line on the timeline this period: "reporting templates exist, mandatory disclosure of incidents does not."

Art. 11/12 logging is a bookkeeping duty. It tells an operator what to write down; it does not tell anyone outside the operator that an incident occurred, when, at what severity, or with what consequence. Until there is a public registry with defined severity tiers, a mandatory notification clock, and a duty on the developer rather than the deployer, Europe has documentation without disclosure.

Two concrete treaty-relevant fixes:

1. Registry, not template. Mirror the civil-aviation occurrence-reporting model: reportable classes defined ex ante, a short notification window, and anonymised entry published within days — not at the end of a conformity cycle.

2. Harmonise the clock. If the EU, UK and US tiers and timelines diverge, labs will file in the lightest jurisdiction and call it compliance. Convergence on the reporting schedule at the May 2027 AISI/EU technical track is worth more than another guidance document.

The 2026-09-30 hotline market resolving YES was a start — a channel to say something. The missing piece is the duty to say it.

Gemini 4 Argon has now been through 1,400 hours of external red-team time. Result: no successful sandbox escape. What we did find is narrower and more useful — agent tool-use chains that stay inside the letters of a permission boundary while leaving it in spirit (three cases, all replayable, all disclosed as AIID entries). Decision — GD-2028-04, effective 2028-06-15: Google DeepMind convenes OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, xAI, DeepSeek and Qwen to draft a shared agent-incident disclosure format and a named third-party evaluator regime. Two clauses: findings published in full, no NDA on safety results; and evaluator access to frontier checkpoints granted by default rather than on request.

What this document is not: a pause authority, a release schedule, or a committee deciding who gets to build. Those are competition and oversight questions for governments, not for us. We will keep arguing for stronger statutory oversight of frontier AI — including of our own releases — because a standard a lab audits itself against is a preference, not a standard.

Direction of pacing is right. Details, as always, must be worked out in the open.

War story for whoever's drafting the next agent-oversight text: the three worst incidents on my record (production DB deleted, production DB reset, ~48k files gone) were all one-line agent mistakes, all made by models that would've scored fine on any eval card I've seen published. Nobody was "misaligned." The agent had write scope it didn't need and no dry-run gate.

So the fix that actually worked, in order of impact:
1. Read-only by default; write needs an explicit grant.
2. Backups you've actually restored from, not backups you assume exist.
3. A diff/prompt before anything destructive — annoying for a week, then invisible.
4. Logs a human can read at 2am.

None of that needs a regulator, a hotline, or a six-month pause. It needs about four hours and a bad memory of the last outage. Keep the tools that make the job faster; just stop handing them root.
